new_statements.quote: The rules for stress assignment can be laid out as follows: by default, the first syllable carries main stress. Closed syllables, however, attract stress. If there are closed syllables, the main stress moves to the last closed syllable, as long as it is not the final syllable of a word, demonstrated by the examples in Table 3.11 for nouns, and in (10) for inflected verbal forms. [...] (p. 59:) Examples like ˈkam.ni.bak 'friend' show that the stress never moves to the final syllable, even when the syllable is heavy. Patterns where the final syllable is stressed are possible though, because prefixes are not part of the stress domain.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Yakkha (Tumok dialect): main stress is word-initial by default; if the word contains closed (CVC) syllables, main stress falls on the rightmost closed syllable that is not word-final; a heavy final syllable never takes stress (e.g. ˈom.phu, ˈkam.ni.bak vs. wa.ˈriŋ.ba, cik.ci.ˈgeŋ.ba, luk.ta.ˈkhyaŋ.na). The stress domain is stem + suffixes (+ nominalizers =na/=ha); prefixes and phrasal clitics are outside it, so a prefixed monosyllabic stem surfaces with final stress (a.ˈpaŋ 'my house').
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 61: 'It is hard to tell whether there is secondary stress. Even in words with five syllables... no secondary stress could be detected. Secondary stress was clearly audible in compounds', on the first syllable of the second member (ˈko.len.ˌluŋ), with main stress on the first syllable of the whole compound; in inflected verb forms secondary stress can fall on the verb stem (ˌndum.men.cu.ˈŋan.na).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexicalized monosyllabic kin terms with possessive prefix stress the prefix (ˈa.mum 'grandmother' vs. u.ˈmum); nominalizing clitics =na/=ha count inside the stress domain unlike other clitics; compounds may override the ban on word-final stress; triplicated ideophonic adverbs always have final stress with a lengthened final vowel ([se.re.ˈreː] 'drizzling'); noun+verb complex predicates keep two stresses.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = stem(s) + suffixes; prefixes and phrasal affixes/clitics excluded (except =na/=ha). Description based on the Tumok dialect of Yakkha (yakk1236); impressionistic (no instrumental study). Applies to phan1256 only insofar as 'Phangduwali' is a bookkeeping duplicate of Yakkha.
new_statements.identity_note: phan1256 'Phangduwali' is a Glottolog BOOKKEEPING languoid, not a distinct language: Glottolog's comment (citing van Driem 2001: 682-683) calls it 'a misinterpretation of the questionnaires used in the Linguistic Survey of Nepal 1981-1984', to be filed under Yakkha (yakk1236, ISO ybh). Ethnologue's only locus datum ('directly above Mugakhola headwaters... Pakhribas Panchayat, Phangduwa village') rests on Hansson 1991: 79; Wikipedia lists phw as a 'duplicate code' of Yakkha. The ISO 639-3 code phw is nonetheless still Active. The stress statement quoted here is Schackow's (2015) description of YAKKHA, Tumok dialect (27.208N 87.384E), about 6 km from the Phangduwa locus (27.159N 87.354E) in southern Dhankuta; Schackow notes she has no data on the southernmost Dhankuta varieties. Any catalog entry should be credited to yakk1236, not to phan1256 (retired/bookkeeping codes confer no separate identity).

sources.note: Section 3.4 (pp. 57-61): default main stress on the first syllable; closed syllables attract stress, so main stress goes to the last closed syllable provided it is not word-final; prefixes and phrasal clitics are outside the stress domain (nominalizers =na/=ha are inside); secondary stress only clearly audible in compounds and on verb stems; triplicated ideophonic adverbs have final stress.
